title: The two-phase shutdown

blocks.text: The page's shutdown idiom has two phases. `shutdown()` stops new work but lets running and queued tasks finish, and `awaitTermination()` waits for them. If they do not finish in time, `shutdownNow()` interrupts the running tasks and returns the ones that never started, and a second `awaitTermination()` waits again. Its edge cases add: if the waiting thread is interrupted, fall back to `shutdownNow()` and re-interrupt the thread.
Write `Shutdown.close(executor, timeout, unit)`, returning the tasks that never started (an empty list when none were dropped):

items: phase 1: `shutdown()`, then wait up to `timeout` for termination;
phase 2, only if phase 1 timed out: `shutdownNow()`, then wait up to `timeout` once more, and return (a task that ignores its interrupt may still be running);
if the calling thread is interrupted while it waits: `shutdownNow()`, restore its interrupt flag, and return what `shutdownNow()` returned.

rows: a running task that ends soon, and two queued tasks
a running task that never ends, and one queued task
the running task was interrupted, and the executor is terminated when `close` returns
a running task that never ends, the caller then interrupted
the caller's interrupt flag is set, the executor terminates

cases.says: A pool whose tasks are done terminates and leaves no task behind.
The first phase stops new work but lets the running and queued tasks finish.
When the first phase times out, the second interrupts the running task, waits for the executor to terminate, and returns the tasks that never started.
A caller interrupted while it waits forces the shutdown and keeps its interrupt flag set.
An interrupted close still returns what shutdownNow() returned: the queued task that never started.
close(executor, 300, MILLISECONDS) reads the timeout in the unit given, so it returns in well under a second per phase.
When a task ignores its interrupt, phase 2 still waits only up to the timeout, then close returns.

concepts: A thread interrupted during awaitTermination() falls back to shutdownNow() and re-interrupts itself.
shutdown() stops new work but finishes running and queued tasks; shutdownNow() interrupts running tasks and returns the ones never started.
The two-phase idiom calls shutdown() and awaitTermination(), and falls back to shutdownNow() when the wait times out.
